name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q01 - Metalloids among Group 15 elements

questiontext.text: Which pair of Group 15 elements consists solely of metalloids?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Down Group 15, metallic character increases as ionisation enthalpy decreases and atomic size increases, transitioning from non-metals to metalloids to metals.

Step 2: Classification of Group 15 Elements
Nitrogen (\(\mathrm{N}\)) and phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P}\)) are non-metals, arsenic (\(\mathrm{As}\)) and antimony (\(\mathrm{Sb}\)) are metalloids, and bismuth (\(\mathrm{Bi}\)) and moscovium (\(\mathrm{Mc}\)) are typical metals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pair consisting solely of metalloids is arsenic (\(\mathrm{As}\)) and antimony (\(\mathrm{Sb}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q02 - General valence shell electronic configuration of p-block elements

questiontext.text: What is the general valence shell electronic configuration of \(p\)-block elements (excluding helium)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In \(p\)-block elements (Groups 13 to 18), the differentiating electron enters the outermost \(p\) subshell while the outermost \(s\) subshell is completely filled.

Step 2: Application
The \(s\) subshell holds 2 electrons (\(ns^2\)) and the \(p\) subshell progressively fills from 1 to 6 electrons (\(np^{1-6}\)). Helium is the only exception, having the \(1s^2\) configuration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The general valence shell electronic configuration of \(p\)-block elements (excluding \(\mathrm{He}\)) is \(ns^2np^{1-6}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q03 - Lewis base behaviour and geometry of ammonia

questiontext.text: Ammonia (\(\mathrm{NH_3}\)) acts as a Lewis base and has a trigonal pyramidal shape because the nitrogen atom possesses:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A Lewis base is an electron-pair donor. The molecular geometry is determined by the total number of bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.

Step 2: Electronic Structure of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\)
Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons, of which 3 are shared in \(\mathrm{N-H}\) covalent bonds and 2 remain as one non-bonding lone pair. This lone pair is available for donation, making \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) a Lewis base, while the three bond pairs and one lone pair give a trigonal pyramidal geometry.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nitrogen atom in \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) possesses three bond pairs and one lone pair of electrons.

answer.text: four bond pairs and no lone pair
two bond pairs and two lone pairs
three bond pairs and one lone pair

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q04 - Most abundant element in the earth's crust

questiontext.text: Which \(p\)-block element is the most abundant of all elements on earth, forming about \(46.6\%\) by mass of the earth's crust?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxygen is the first member of Group 16 (chalcogens) and occurs extensively in silicates, oxides, water, and the atmosphere.

Step 2: Quantitative Fact
Oxygen accounts for about \(46.6\%\) by mass of the earth's crust and \(20.946\%\) by volume of dry air.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Oxygen is the most abundant element in the earth's crust.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q05 - Colour and odour of chlorine gas

questiontext.text: Which physical description correctly matches chlorine gas (\(\mathrm{Cl_2}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halogens absorb visible radiation corresponding to electronic transitions between outer levels, imparting characteristic colours.

Step 2: Properties of Chlorine
Chlorine is a greenish yellow gas with a pungent and suffocating odour, about 2–5 times heavier than air, and liquefies into a greenish yellow liquid boiling at \(239\ \mathrm{K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chlorine is a greenish yellow gas with a pungent and suffocating odour.

answer.text: Greenish yellow gas with a pungent and suffocating odour
Pale blue gas with a characteristic smell
Colourless gas with a rotten fish smell
Reddish brown gas with a sweet odour

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q06 - Lowest boiling point among known substances

questiontext.text: Which noble gas has the lowest boiling point (\(4.2\ \mathrm{K}\)) of any known substance?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Noble gases are monoatomic and interact solely through weak dispersion (London) forces, which decrease with decreasing atomic size and polarisability.

Step 2: Comparison
Helium (\(\mathrm{He}\)) is the smallest and lightest noble gas, so its interatomic dispersion forces are minimal, giving it a boiling point of \(4.2\ \mathrm{K}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Helium has the lowest boiling point (\(4.2\ \mathrm{K}\)) of any known substance.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q07 - Major noble gas constituent in dry air

questiontext.text: Noble gases together constitute about \(1\%\) by volume of dry air. Which noble gas is the major constituent among them?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All noble gases except radon and oganesson occur naturally in the atmosphere, with varying abundances.

Step 2: Atmospheric Abundance
Dry air contains approximately \(0.934\%\) argon by volume, making argon by far the major noble gas constituent in the atmosphere.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Argon is the major noble gas constituent of dry air.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q08 - Composition of aqua regia

questiontext.text: Aqua regia, used for dissolving noble metals such as gold and platinum, is prepared by mixing:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Noble metals like gold and platinum do not dissolve in concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) or \(\mathrm{HCl}\) alone, but dissolve in aqua regia through combined oxidation by \(\mathrm{NO_3^-}\) and complexation by \(\mathrm{Cl^-}\).

Step 2: Composition
Aqua regia is a freshly prepared mixture of three parts of concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and one part of concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Aqua regia consists of three parts concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and one part concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\).

answer.text: one part concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and three parts concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
three parts concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) and one part concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)
one part concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and one part concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)
three parts concentrated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and one part concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q09 - Chemical formula of fluorapatite

questiontext.text: Phosphorus occurs in phosphate rocks as minerals of the apatite family. Which formula represents fluorapatite?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Apatite minerals have the general composition \(\mathrm{Ca_9(PO_4)_6 \cdot CaX_2}\), where \(\mathrm{X}\) can be \(\mathrm{F}\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\), or \(\mathrm{OH}\).

Step 2: Substitution
Setting \(\mathrm{X = F}\) gives the formula for fluorapatite as \(\mathrm{Ca_9(PO_4)_6 \cdot CaF_2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fluorapatite is represented by \(\mathrm{Ca_9(PO_4)_6 \cdot CaF_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q10 - Transition temperature between rhombic and monoclinic sulphur

questiontext.text: At what transition temperature are both rhombic (\(\alpha\)-sulphur) and monoclinic (\(\beta\)-sulphur) allotropes of sulphur stable?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Rhombic sulphur (\(\alpha\)-sulphur) is stable below the transition temperature and transforms into monoclinic sulphur (\(\beta\)-sulphur) above it.

Step 2: Value Recall
At \(369\ \mathrm{K}\), both \(\alpha\)-sulphur and \(\beta\)-sulphur are stable and coexist in equilibrium.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The transition temperature between rhombic and monoclinic sulphur is \(369\ \mathrm{K}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q11 - Most electronegative element in the periodic table

questiontext.text: Which element has the highest electronegativity in the periodic table and exhibits only the \(-1\) oxidation state in its compounds?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electronegativity decreases down Group 17 as atomic size increases. Small atomic size and high effective nuclear charge give the top member the strongest attraction for shared electrons.

Step 2: Application
Fluorine has the highest electronegativity (4.0 on the Pauling scale) of all elements and lacks \(d\)-orbitals, so it exhibits only the \(-1\) oxidation state.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Fluorine is the most electronegative element and exhibits only the \(-1\) oxidation state.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q12 - Chemical formula of oleum

questiontext.text: In the Contact Process, sulphur trioxide (\(\mathrm{SO_3}\)) is absorbed in concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) to produce oleum. What is the chemical formula of oleum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Direct absorption of \(\mathrm{SO_3}\) in water forms a dense mist of sulphuric acid, so \(\mathrm{SO_3}\) is instead absorbed in concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).

Step 2: Chemical Equation
\(\mathrm{SO_3 + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow H_2S_2O_7}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Oleum (pyrosulphuric acid) has the chemical formula \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q13 - Absence of pentahalides in nitrogen

questiontext.text: Although nitrogen exhibits a \(+5\) oxidation state in oxo-species, it does not form any pentahalide such as \(\mathrm{NCl_5}\). Why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Forming a pentahalide \(\mathrm{EX_5}\) requires the central atom to expand its valence shell beyond an octet to accommodate five covalent bonds.

Step 2: Orbital Availability
Nitrogen belongs to the second period (\(n = 2\)) and has only one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals available for bonding. Due to the absence of \(2d\) orbitals, its maximum covalency is restricted to 4.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Nitrogen does not form pentahalides because it lacks \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell to expand its covalency beyond four.

answer.text: Nitrogen lacks \(d\)-orbitals in its valence shell to expand its covalency beyond four.
Nitrogen has a very low ionisation enthalpy.
Nitrogen has a strong inert pair effect.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q14 - Weakness of single N-N bond compared to P-P bond

questiontext.text: Why is the single \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond weaker than the single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bond, resulting in weaker catenation tendency in nitrogen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Catenation tendency depends on the strength of the homonuclear single bond (\(\mathrm{E-E}\)).

Step 2: Electronic Repulsion Analysis
Nitrogen has a very small atomic radius, so the \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond length is short. This brings the non-bonding lone pairs on the two nitrogen atoms close together, causing high interelectronic repulsion that weakens the \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond relative to the longer \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond is weaker than \(\mathrm{P-P}\) due to high interelectronic repulsion of non-bonding electrons owing to the small bond length.

answer.text: Nitrogen has vacant \(d\)-orbitals that destabilise single bonds.
High interelectronic repulsion of non-bonding electrons due to the small \(\mathrm{N-N}\) bond length.
Phosphorus forms stronger \(p\pi-p\pi\) multiple bonds than nitrogen.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q15 - Preparation of very pure dinitrogen

questiontext.text: Very pure dinitrogen gas (\(\mathrm{N_2}\)) is obtained in the laboratory by the thermal decomposition of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different laboratory methods yield dinitrogen of varying purity depending on whether side products like \(\mathrm{NO}\) or \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) are formed.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reactions
Thermal decomposition of sodium or barium azide yields only the metal and pure dinitrogen gas: \(\mathrm{Ba(N_3)_2 \rightarrow Ba + 3N_2}\) and \(2\mathrm{NaN_3 \rightarrow 2Na + 3N_2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Very pure dinitrogen is obtained by the thermal decomposition of sodium or barium azide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q16 - Thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate

questiontext.text: What are the products formed upon thermal decomposition of ammonium dichromate, \((\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{Cr_2O_7}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ammonium dichromate undergoes an intramolecular redox decomposition on heating in which \(\mathrm{NH_4^+}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{N_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Cr(VI)}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cr(III)}\).

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\((\mathrm{NH_4})_2\mathrm{Cr_2O_7} \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \mathrm{N_2 + 4H_2O + Cr_2O_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The products formed are \(\mathrm{N_2}\), \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), and \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q17 - Reaction of aqueous Cu2+ with ammonia

questiontext.text: When aqueous ammonia is added to a blue solution of \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}(aq)\), a deep blue colour is obtained due to the formation of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ammonia acts as a Lewis base by donating its lone pair of electrons to transition metal ions to form coordination complexes.

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq) + 4NH_3(aq) \rightleftharpoons [Cu(NH_3)_4]^{2+}(aq)}\), which imparts a deep blue colour to the solution.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The deep blue colour is due to the formation of \([\mathrm{Cu(NH_3)_4}]^{2+}(aq)\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q18 - Dimerisation of nitrogen dioxide

questiontext.text: Why does \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) readily dimerise to \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) on cooling?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Molecules containing an odd number of valence electrons possess an unpaired electron and tend to dimerise to achieve a paired, more stable electronic configuration.

Step 2: Electron Count
\(\mathrm{NO_2}\) has \(5 + 2(6) = 17\) valence electrons (an odd-electron molecule). On dimerisation, two \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) molecules pair their odd electrons to form a stable \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) molecule with 34 (even) valence electrons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{NO_2}\) dimerises because it contains an odd number of valence electrons and converts into stable \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) with an even number of electrons.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) has a linear structure that is unstable at low temperature.
\(\mathrm{NO_2}\) is an odd-electron molecule that pairs up to form stable \(\mathrm{N_2O_4}\) with even electrons.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q19 - Passivity of metals in concentrated nitric acid

questiontext.text: Which pair of metals does NOT dissolve in concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) due to the formation of a passive oxide film on the surface?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent that attacks most metals, except noble metals like \(\mathrm{Au}\) and \(\mathrm{Pt}\), or metals that form an impervious protective oxide layer.

Step 2: Identification of Passive Metals
Chromium (\(\mathrm{Cr}\)) and aluminium (\(\mathrm{Al}\)) do not dissolve in concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) because of the formation of a passive film of oxide on their surfaces.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{Cr}\) and \(\mathrm{Al}\) do not dissolve in concentrated \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\) due to oxide passivity.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q20 - High reactivity of white phosphorus

questiontext.text: White phosphorus is much more reactive than red phosphorus under normal conditions primarily because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
White phosphorus consists of discrete tetrahedral \(\mathrm{P_4}\) molecules, whereas red phosphorus is polymeric with chains of linked \(\mathrm{P_4}\) tetrahedra.

Step 2: Structural Strain Analysis
In the discrete tetrahedral \(\mathrm{P_4}\) molecule, the \(\mathrm{P-P-P}\) bond angles are only \(60^\circ\), which introduces considerable angular strain and makes white phosphorus less stable and highly reactive.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
White phosphorus is more reactive due to angular strain in the \(\mathrm{P_4}\) molecule where the bond angles are only \(60^\circ\).

answer.text: of angular strain in the \(\mathrm{P_4}\) molecule with \(60^\circ\) bond angles

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q21 - Reaction of white phosphorus with boiling NaOH

questiontext.text: When white phosphorus is heated with concentrated \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution in an inert atmosphere of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), the products formed are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
White phosphorus undergoes disproportionation in boiling alkali, being simultaneously reduced to phosphine (\(-3\) oxidation state) and oxidised to hypophosphite (\(+1\) oxidation state).

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\(\mathrm{P_4 + 3NaOH + 3H_2O \rightarrow PH_3 + 3NaH_2PO_2}\) (sodium hypophosphite).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The products formed are \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{NaH_2PO_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q22 - Chemicals used in Holme's signals

questiontext.text: In Holme's signals used at sea, containers pierced and thrown into water contain which pair of compounds to generate spontaneously combustible gases?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Holme's signals rely on the spontaneous combustion of impure phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH_3}\) containing \(\mathrm{P_2H_4}\)) and acetylene (\(\mathrm{C_2H_2}\)) produced upon contact with water.

Step 2: Identification of Reagents
Calcium carbide (\(\mathrm{CaC_2}\)) reacts with water to produce acetylene, while calcium phosphide (\(\mathrm{Ca_3P_2}\)) reacts with water to produce phosphine, which ignites spontaneously and burns acetylene as a bright signal.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The containers in Holme's signals contain calcium carbide and calcium phosphide.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q23 - Hydrolysis of phosphorus trichloride

questiontext.text: Phosphorus trichloride (\(\mathrm{PCl_3}\)) fumes in moist air because it hydrolyses to form:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Non-metal halides in the \(+3\) oxidation state hydrolyse in moisture to form the corresponding \(+3\) oxoacid and hydrogen halide.

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\(\mathrm{PCl_3 + 3H_2O \rightarrow H_3PO_3 + 3HCl}\). The liberated \(\mathrm{HCl}\) gas produces white fumes in moist air.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{PCl_3}\) hydrolyses to form \(\mathrm{H_3PO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q24 - Axial vs equatorial bond lengths in PCl5

questiontext.text: In the gaseous and liquid phases, \(\mathrm{PCl_5}\) has a trigonal bipyramidal structure. Which statement about its \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In a trigonal bipyramidal (\(sp^3d\)) geometry, the three equatorial bonds lie in a plane at \(120^\circ\) to each other, whereas the two axial bonds lie perpendicular to the equatorial plane at \(90^\circ\) to the three equatorial bonds.

Step 2: Repulsion Analysis
Each axial bond pair suffers three \(90^\circ\) repulsions from the equatorial bond pairs, which is greater than the repulsions experienced by equatorial bond pairs. Consequently, the two axial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds are longer (\(240\ \mathrm{pm}\)) than the three equivalent equatorial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds (\(202\ \mathrm{pm}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two axial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds are longer than the three equivalent equatorial \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds.

answer.text: All five \(\mathrm{P-Cl}\) bonds are identical in length.
The three equatorial bonds are longer than the two axial bonds.
The two axial bonds are shorter because they experience fewer repulsions.
The two axial bonds are longer than the three equivalent equatorial bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q25 - Basicity and reducing character of H3PO2

questiontext.text: Hypophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\)) is a strong reducing agent and is monobasic because its molecule contains:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In phosphorus oxoacids, only hydrogen atoms attached to oxygen (\(\mathrm{P-OH}\)) are ionisable and determine basicity, while hydrogen atoms bonded directly to phosphorus (\(\mathrm{P-H}\)) are non-ionisable and impart reducing character.

Step 2: Structure of \(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\)
\(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\) contains one \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) bond (making it monobasic), two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds (making it a strong reducing agent), and one \(\mathrm{P=O}\) bond.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H_3PO_2}\) contains one \(\mathrm{P-OH}\) bond and two \(\mathrm{P-H}\) bonds.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q26 - Disproportionation of orthophosphorous acid on heating

questiontext.text: On heating, orthophosphorous acid (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_3}\)) undergoes disproportionation to yield:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Oxoacids of phosphorus in intermediate oxidation states (such as \(+3\) in \(\mathrm{H_3PO_3}\)) disproportionate on heating into higher (\(+5\)) and lower (\(-3\)) oxidation states.

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\(4\mathrm{H_3PO_3} \rightarrow 3\mathrm{H_3PO_4} + \mathrm{PH_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Heating \(\mathrm{H_3PO_3}\) yields orthophosphoric acid (\(\mathrm{H_3PO_4}\)) and phosphine (\(\mathrm{PH_3}\)).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q27 - Lower first ionisation enthalpy of Group 16 vs Group 15

questiontext.text: Why do Group 16 elements generally have lower first ionisation enthalpy than the corresponding Group 15 elements in the same period?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ionisation enthalpy depends on nuclear charge, atomic size, and the stability of the electronic configuration.

Step 2: Electronic Configuration Comparison
Group 15 elements have an extra stable half-filled \(np^3\) configuration, requiring more energy to remove an electron. Group 16 elements have an \(np^4\) configuration, where removing one electron relieves interelectronic repulsion in the doubly occupied \(p\) orbital and leaves a stable half-filled \(np^3\) configuration.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Group 15 elements possess extra stable half-filled \(p\)-orbital electronic configurations, so removing an electron from them requires more energy than from Group 16 elements.

answer.text: Group 16 elements have larger atomic radii than Group 15 elements.
Group 16 elements have lower effective nuclear charge.
Group 15 elements have extra stable half-filled \(p\)-orbital electronic configurations.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q28 - Paramagnetic form of sulphur in vapour state

questiontext.text: At elevated temperatures (\(\sim 1000\ \mathrm{K}\)) in the vapour state, sulphur exhibits paramagnetic behaviour due to the dominant presence of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Paramagnetism arises from the presence of unpaired electrons in molecular orbitals.

Step 2: Molecular Species at High Temperature
At \(\sim 1000\ \mathrm{K}\) in the vapour state, sulphur exists dominantly as \(\mathrm{S_2}\) molecules. Like \(\mathrm{O_2}\), the \(\mathrm{S_2}\) molecule has two unpaired electrons in its antibonding \(\pi^*\) molecular orbitals, making it paramagnetic.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The paramagnetic behaviour of sulphur vapour at \(\sim 1000\ \mathrm{K}\) is due to \(\mathrm{S_2}\) molecules.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q29 - Hybridisation and molecular geometry of SF4

questiontext.text: What is the hybridisation of sulphur and the molecular geometry of \(\mathrm{SF_4}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to VSEPR theory, the hybridisation and geometry depend on the total number of bond pairs and lone pairs on the central atom.

Step 2: Electron Pair Count in \(\mathrm{SF_4}\)
Sulphur has 6 valence electrons; 4 form \(\mathrm{S-F}\) single bonds and 2 remain as 1 lone pair. Five electron pairs correspond to \(sp^3d\) hybridisation (trigonal bipyramidal electron arrangement) with the lone pair occupying an equatorial position, giving a see-saw geometry.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{SF_4}\) has \(sp^3d\) hybridisation and a see-saw geometry.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q30 - Use of silent electrical discharge in ozone preparation

questiontext.text: Why is a silent electrical discharge used when preparing ozone from dioxygen?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The conversion of dioxygen to ozone is an endothermic process: \(3\mathrm{O_2 \rightarrow 2O_3},\ \Delta H^\circ(298\ \mathrm{K}) = +142\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

Step 2: Effect of Heat/Sparking
Ozone is thermodynamically unstable and decomposes back into \(\mathrm{O_2}\) when heated or subjected to sparking. A silent electrical discharge supplies the needed energy without generating excessive heat or sparks, thereby preventing decomposition of the ozone formed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Silent electrical discharge is used to prevent the decomposition of ozone since its formation from oxygen is endothermic.

answer.text: To prevent the decomposition of ozone, as its formation is endothermic
To convert ozone directly into a solid

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q31 - Quantitative estimation of ozone

questiontext.text: Ozone is estimated quantitatively by reacting it with excess \(\mathrm{KI}\) solution buffered with a borate buffer (\(\mathrm{pH}\ 9.2\)) and titrating the liberated iodine against a standard solution of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ozone oxidises iodide ions (\(\mathrm{I^-}\)) in buffered aqueous solution to molecular iodine (\(\mathrm{I_2}\)): \(2\mathrm{I^-(aq) + H_2O(l) + O_3(g) \rightarrow 2OH^-(aq) + I_2(s) + O_2(g)}\).

Step 2: Titration Reagent
The liberated iodine is quantitatively titrated against a standard solution of sodium thiosulphate (\(\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The liberated iodine is titrated against a standard solution of sodium thiosulphate.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q32 - Detection test for sulphur dioxide gas

questiontext.text: When moist \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas is passed through an acidified potassium permanganate(VII) solution, what is observed?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Moist sulphur dioxide acts as a reducing agent, reducing \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) (purple) to \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) (colourless) while being oxidised to \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\).

Step 2: Balanced Ionic Equation
\(5\mathrm{SO_2 + 2MnO_4^- + 2H_2O \rightarrow 5SO_4^{2-} + 4H^+ + 2Mn^{2+}}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The purple acidified potassium permanganate(VII) solution is decolourised, which serves as a convenient test for \(\mathrm{SO_2}\).

answer.text: A yellow precipitate of sulphur is formed.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q33 - Dehydrating action of concentrated sulphuric acid on carbohydrates

questiontext.text: Concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) chars cane sugar (\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}}\)) to a black mass of carbon because concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) acts as a strong:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Concentrated sulphuric acid has a very strong affinity for water and removes the elements of water (\(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{O}\) in a 2:1 ratio) from organic compounds such as carbohydrates.

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11} \xrightarrow{H_2SO_4} 12C + 11H_2O}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The charring action on carbohydrates is due to the strong dehydrating nature of concentrated \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q34 - Comparison of Ka1 and Ka2 of H2SO4 in water

questiontext.text: For the ionisation of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) in aqueous solution, \(K_{a_2} \ll K_{a_1}\) because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) ionises in water in two steps: first to \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\) and \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\) (\(K_{a_1} > 10\)), and then \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\) ionises to \(\mathrm{H_3O^+}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\) (\(K_{a_2} = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\)).

Step 2: Electrostatic Explanation
\(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) is a neutral molecule and a very strong acid that dissociates almost completely in the first step. Removing a positively charged proton (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)) from the negatively charged \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\) ion is much harder due to electrostatic attraction, making the second ionisation very small.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(K_{a_2} \ll K_{a_1}\) because the first ionisation of neutral \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) is very large while the dissociation of the negatively charged \(\mathrm{HSO_4^-}\) ion is much smaller.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q35 - Reaction of chlorine with cold and dilute NaOH

questiontext.text: When chlorine gas reacts with cold and dilute \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) solution, the products formed are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chlorine undergoes disproportionation in aqueous alkali, and the oxidised product depends on temperature and alkali concentration.

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
With cold and dilute \(\mathrm{NaOH}\): \(2\mathrm{NaOH} + \mathrm{Cl_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{NaOCl} + \mathrm{H_2O}\) (chloride and hypochlorite).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The products formed are \(\mathrm{NaCl}\), \(\mathrm{NaOCl}\), and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q36 - Mechanism of bleaching action of chlorine

questiontext.text: The bleaching action of chlorine in the presence of moisture is permanent because it is due to:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chlorine reacts with water to form hydrochloric acid and hypochlorous acid (\(\mathrm{HOCl}\)), which decomposes to liberate nascent oxygen: \(\mathrm{Cl_2 + H_2O \rightarrow 2HCl + O}\).

Step 2: Bleaching Process
The nascent oxygen oxidises coloured vegetable or organic matter to colourless substances. Since it involves oxidation, the bleaching effect of chlorine is permanent.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The permanent bleaching action of chlorine is due to oxidation by nascent oxygen.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q37 - Reaction of finely powdered iron with HCl

questiontext.text: When \(\mathrm{HCl}\) reacts with finely powdered iron, it forms ferrous chloride (\(\mathrm{FeCl_2}\)) and not ferric chloride (\(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\)). Why?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Iron reacts with hydrochloric acid according to \(\mathrm{Fe + 2HCl \rightarrow FeCl_2 + H_2}\).

Step 2: Role of Liberated Hydrogen
The hydrogen gas liberated during the reaction creates a reducing environment that prevents the oxidation of \(\mathrm{FeCl_2}\) to \(\mathrm{FeCl_3}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Liberation of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas prevents the formation of ferric chloride.

answer.text: Liberation of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) prevents the formation of ferric chloride.
\(\mathrm{HCl}\) is a stronger oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\).
Iron forms a passive oxide film in \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q38 - Higher reactivity of ICl compared to I2

questiontext.text: Why is the interhalogen compound \(\mathrm{ICl}\) more reactive than molecular iodine (\(\mathrm{I_2}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Interhalogen compounds \(\mathrm{XX'}\) are generally more reactive than the constituent halogens (except fluorine) because the heteronuclear \(\mathrm{X-X'}\) bond is weaker than the homonuclear \(\mathrm{X-X}\) bond (except \(\mathrm{F-F}\)).

Step 2: Application
The \(\mathrm{I-Cl}\) bond in \(\mathrm{ICl}\) is weaker than the \(\mathrm{I-I}\) bond in \(\mathrm{I_2}\), so \(\mathrm{ICl}\) dissociates and reacts more readily.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{ICl}\) is more reactive than \(\mathrm{I_2}\) because the \(\mathrm{I-Cl}\) bond is weaker than the \(\mathrm{I-I}\) bond.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{ICl}\) is an ionic compound whereas \(\mathrm{I_2}\) is covalent.
The \(\mathrm{I-Cl}\) bond is weaker than the \(\mathrm{I-I}\) bond.
\(\mathrm{ICl}\) has a higher bond dissociation enthalpy than \(\mathrm{I_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q39 - Neil Bartlett's first xenon compound

questiontext.text: What inspired Neil Bartlett to carry out the reaction between xenon and \(\mathrm{PtF_6}\), leading to the first noble gas compound?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Neil Bartlett first prepared the red ionic compound \(\mathrm{O_2^+[PtF_6]^-}\) by reacting \(\mathrm{O_2}\) with \(\mathrm{PtF_6}\).

Step 2: Ionisation Enthalpy Comparison
He noticed that the first ionisation enthalpy of molecular oxygen (\(1175\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) is almost identical to that of xenon (\(1170\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)), which inspired him to prepare the analogous red compound \(\mathrm{Xe^+[PtF_6]^-}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Bartlett was inspired by the nearly identical first ionisation enthalpies of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Xe}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q40 - Non-redox nature of XeF6 hydrolysis

questiontext.text: Which statement is true regarding the partial and complete hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\) with water?

generalfeedback.text:

A redox reaction involves a change in the oxidation states of one or more elements between reactants and products.

Step 2: Oxidation State Check
In \(\mathrm{XeF_6 + H_2O \rightarrow XeOF_4 + 2HF}\), \(\mathrm{XeF_6 + 2H_2O \rightarrow XeO_2F_2 + 4HF}\), and \(\mathrm{XeF_6 + 3H_2O \rightarrow XeO_3 + 6HF}\), xenon remains in the \(+6\) oxidation state, oxygen in \(-2\), hydrogen in \(+1\), and fluorine in \(-1\). None of the oxidation states change.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\) is a non-redox reaction in which the oxidation states of all elements remain unchanged.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q41 - Higher boiling point of NH3 than PH3

questiontext.text: Why does \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) have a higher boiling point (\(238.5\ \mathrm{K}\)) than \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) (\(185.5\ \mathrm{K}\)) despite having a lower molecular mass?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boiling point increases with the strength of intermolecular attractive forces.

Step 2: Intermolecular Interaction Comparison
Because nitrogen is small and highly electronegative, \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) molecules are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding in the liquid state, whereas \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) molecules do not form hydrogen bonds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{NH_3}\) has a higher boiling point than \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding in \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).

answer.text: \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) molecules are associated through intermolecular hydrogen bonding.
\(\mathrm{PH_3}\) has stronger van der Waals forces than \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).
\(\mathrm{PH_3}\) is a linear molecule with zero dipole moment.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q42 - Acidic strength trend of Group 16 hydrides

questiontext.text: Why is \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) less acidic than \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\) in aqueous solution?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For hydrides of the type \(\mathrm{H_2E}\) in Group 16, acidic strength increases as the \(\mathrm{H-E}\) bond becomes easier to cleave.

Step 2: Bond Dissociation Enthalpy Trend
Down Group 16 from \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) to \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\), the atomic size of \(\mathrm{E}\) increases and the \(\mathrm{H-E}\) bond dissociation enthalpy decreases (from \(347\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) in \(\mathrm{H_2S}\) to \(238\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) in \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{H_2S}\) is less acidic than \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\) because the \(\mathrm{H-E}\) bond dissociation enthalpy decreases down the group.

answer.text: Electronegativity of \(\mathrm{Te}\) is higher than that of \(\mathrm{S}\).
The \(\mathrm{H-E}\) bond dissociation enthalpy decreases down Group 16.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q43 - Existence of R3P=O but not R3N=O

questiontext.text: Why does \(\mathrm{R_3P=O}\) exist whereas \(\mathrm{R_3N=O}\) does not (where \(\mathrm{R}\) is an alkyl group)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Forming \(\mathrm{R_3E=O}\) requires the central atom \(\mathrm{E}\) to form three \(\sigma\) bonds with \(\mathrm{R}\) groups, one \(\sigma\) bond with oxygen, and an additional \(d\pi-p\pi\) multiple bond with oxygen, giving a covalency of 5.

Step 2: Orbital Availability
Phosphorus has vacant \(3d\) orbitals and can expand its covalency beyond 4 to form a \(d\pi-p\pi\) bond with oxygen. Nitrogen lacks \(d\)-orbitals, restricting its maximum covalency to 4 and preventing \(d\pi-p\pi\) bonding.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{R_3P=O}\) exists because phosphorus has vacant \(d\)-orbitals to form a \(d\pi-p\pi\) bond, whereas nitrogen lacks \(d\)-orbitals.

answer.text: Nitrogen cannot form \(\sigma\) bonds with alkyl groups.
Phosphorus has vacant \(d\)-orbitals to form \(d\pi-p\pi\) bonds, whereas nitrogen lacks \(d\)-orbitals.
Nitrogen has a larger atomic size than phosphorus.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q44 - Stability of oxidation states in bismuth due to inert pair effect

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the oxidation state stability of bismuth in Group 15?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Down Group 15, the stability of the \(+5\) oxidation state decreases while that of the \(+3\) oxidation state increases due to the inert pair effect (reluctance of the \(ns^2\) electron pair to participate in bonding).

Step 2: Application to Bismuth
Bismuth hardly forms any compound in the \(-3\) oxidation state and its \(+3\) state is much more stable than \(+5\). The only well-characterised \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) compound is \(\mathrm{BiF_5}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Due to the inert pair effect, \(\mathrm{Bi(+3)}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{Bi(+5)}\), and \(\mathrm{BiF_5}\) is the only well-characterised \(\mathrm{Bi(V)}\) compound.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{Bi(+5)}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{Bi(+3)}\) and forms all pentahalides.
\(\mathrm{Bi(-3)}\) is the most stable oxidation state of bismuth.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q45 - Bond angle comparison between PH4+ and PH3

questiontext.text: Why is the \(\mathrm{H-P-H}\) bond angle in \(\mathrm{PH_4^+}\) higher than that in \(\mathrm{PH_3}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to VSEPR theory, lone pair–bond pair repulsion is greater than bond pair–bond pair repulsion, which compresses bond angles in molecules containing lone pairs.

Step 2: Hybridisation and Electron Pairs
Both \(\mathrm{PH_4^+}\) and \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) are \(sp^3\) hybridised. In \(\mathrm{PH_4^+}\), all four orbitals are bonded (four bond pairs, zero lone pairs), giving a regular tetrahedral angle of \(109^\circ 28'\). In \(\mathrm{PH_3}\), there are three bond pairs and one lone pair; lone pair–bond pair repulsion compresses the \(\mathrm{H-P-H}\) angle to \(93.6^\circ\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{PH_4^+}\) has four bond pairs and no lone pair, whereas \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) has one lone pair whose repulsion compresses the bond angle.

answer.text: \(\mathrm{PH_4^+}\) has four bond pairs and no lone pair, whereas \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) has a lone pair causing lone pair–bond pair repulsion.
Phosphorus is more electronegative in \(\mathrm{PH_3}\) than in \(\mathrm{PH_4^+}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q46 - Oxidation states of phosphorus in five compounds

questiontext.text: What are the oxidation states of phosphorus in \(\mathrm{H_3PO_3,\ PCl_3,\ Ca_3P_2,\ Na_3PO_4,}\) and \(\mathrm{POF_3}\) respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Rules
Use standard oxidation numbers: \(\mathrm{H} = +1\), \(\mathrm{O} = -2\), \(\mathrm{Cl} = -1\), \(\mathrm{F} = -1\), \(\mathrm{Na} = +1\), \(\mathrm{Ca} = +2\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Calculation
1. \(\mathrm{H_3PO_3}\): \(3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +3\).
2. \(\mathrm{PCl_3}\): \(x + 3(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +3\).
3. \(\mathrm{Ca_3P_2}\): \(3(+2) + 2x = 0 \Rightarrow x = -3\).
4. \(\mathrm{Na_3PO_4}\): \(3(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5\).
5. \(\mathrm{POF_3}\): \(x + (-2) + 3(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The oxidation states of phosphorus are \(+3, +3, -3, +5, +5\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q47 - Atomicity difference between nitrogen and phosphorus

questiontext.text: Nitrogen exists as a diatomic molecule (\(\mathrm{N_2}\)) whereas phosphorus exists as a tetraatomic molecule (\(\mathrm{P_4}\)). What is the fundamental reason for this difference?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Effective \(p\pi-p\pi\) multiple bonding requires compact \(2p\) orbitals of similar energy and small internuclear distance.

Step 2: Orbital Overlap Comparison
Nitrogen is small and forms strong \(p\pi-p\pi\) multiple bonds with itself, giving a very stable \(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\) triple bond (bond enthalpy \(941.4\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) in diatomic \(\mathrm{N_2}\). Phosphorus has larger, more diffuse \(3p\) orbitals that cannot overlap effectively to form \(p\pi-p\pi\) bonds, so it forms single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bonds in a discrete tetrahedral \(\mathrm{P_4}\) molecule.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Nitrogen forms strong \(p\pi-p\pi\) triple bonds to exist as \(\mathrm{N_2}\), while phosphorus forms single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bonds to exist as \(\mathrm{P_4}\).

answer.text: Phosphorus has a higher electronegativity than nitrogen.
Nitrogen forms strong \(p\pi-p\pi\) multiple bonds (\(\mathrm{N\equiv N}\)), whereas phosphorus forms single \(\mathrm{P-P}\) bonds due to larger, diffuse orbitals.
The \(\mathrm{N-N}\) single bond is stronger than the \(\mathrm{P-P}\) single bond.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q48 - Covalence of nitrogen in N2O5

questiontext.text: What is the covalence of each nitrogen atom in dinitrogen pentoxide (\(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Covalence is the number of covalent bonds (shared electron pairs) formed by an atom, which for nitrogen cannot exceed 4 due to the availability of only one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals.

Step 2: Structure of \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\)
In \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) (\(\mathrm{O_2N-O-NO_2}\)), each nitrogen atom is bonded to one bridging oxygen via a single bond, one terminal oxygen via a double bond, and another terminal oxygen via a coordinate (dative) single bond, making a total of 4 covalent bonds per nitrogen atom.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The covalence of nitrogen in \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) is 4.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q49 - Formation of O2- oxides despite endothermic second electron gain enthalpy

questiontext.text: Although the electron gain enthalpy for \(\mathrm{O \rightarrow O^{2-}}\) is overall endothermic (\(-141 + 702 = +561\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)), a large number of ionic oxides contain \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) rather than \(\mathrm{O^-}\) because:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The thermodynamic stability of an ionic solid depends on the overall Born–Haber cycle, where lattice enthalpy plays a decisive role.

Step 2: Lattice Energy Comparison
Because \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) carries twice the charge of \(\mathrm{O^-}\), the lattice energy released when \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) combines with metal cations is much higher than for \(\mathrm{O^-}\), easily compensating for the endothermic second electron gain enthalpy.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The high lattice energy of oxides containing \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) more than compensates for the endothermic second electron gain enthalpy.

answer.text: the high lattice energy of \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\) compounds compensates for the endothermic electron gain
\(\mathrm{O^-}\) has a larger ionic radius than \(\mathrm{O^{2-}}\)
oxygen has a very low first ionisation enthalpy

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q50 - Thermodynamic instability of ozone

questiontext.text: Why is ozone (\(\mathrm{O_3}\)) thermodynamically unstable with respect to dioxygen (\(\mathrm{O_2}\)) and potentially explosive at high concentrations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Thermodynamic spontaneity is governed by Gibbs energy change, \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\).

Step 2: Signs of \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta S\) for \(2\mathrm{O_3 \rightarrow 3O_2}\)
Decomposition of ozone into oxygen liberates heat (\(\Delta H < 0\)) and increases the number of gas molecules from 2 to 3, increasing entropy (\(\Delta S > 0\)). Both effects reinforce each other to produce a large negative \(\Delta G\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Its decomposition into oxygen has \(\Delta H < 0\) and \(\Delta S > 0\), resulting in a large negative \(\Delta G\).

answer.text: Its decomposition into oxygen has \(\Delta H > 0\) and \(\Delta S < 0\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q51 - Ring shapes of S8 and cyclo-S6

questiontext.text: Which pair correctly describes the ring conformations of \(\mathrm{S_8}\) (in rhombic/monoclinic sulphur) and cyclo-\(\mathrm{S_6}\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Elemental sulphur forms puckered cyclic molecules to minimise lone pair–lone pair repulsions and maintain optimal \(\mathrm{S-S-S}\) bond angles.

Step 2: Conformations
The \(\mathrm{S_8}\) ring in both rhombic and monoclinic sulphur adopts a puckered crown shape, whereas cyclo-\(\mathrm{S_6}\) adopts a chair form.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{S_8}\) has a crown shape and cyclo-\(\mathrm{S_6}\) has a chair form.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q52 - Reason F2 is a stronger oxidising agent than Cl2

questiontext.text: Although fluorine has a less negative electron gain enthalpy than chlorine, \(\mathrm{F_2}\) is a much stronger oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) in aqueous solution because of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The oxidising power of a halogen \(\mathrm{X_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{X^-(aq)}\) depends on three thermodynamic steps: \(\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\mathrm{diss}}H^\circ(\mathrm{X_2})\), \(\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}}H^\circ(\mathrm{X})\), and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{hyd}}H^\circ(\mathrm{X^-})\).

Step 2: Comparison of \(\mathrm{F_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\)
Even though \(\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}}H^\circ\) of \(\mathrm{F}\) (\(-333\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) is slightly less negative than \(\mathrm{Cl}\) (\(-349\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)), \(\mathrm{F_2}\) has a much lower bond dissociation enthalpy (\(158.8\) vs \(242.6\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) and \(\mathrm{F^-}\) has a much higher hydration enthalpy (\(515\) vs \(381\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{F_2}\) is a stronger oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) due to low \(\mathrm{F-F}\) bond dissociation enthalpy and high hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{F^-}\).

answer.text: high \(\mathrm{F-F}\) bond dissociation enthalpy and low hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{F^-}\)
lower ionisation enthalpy of fluorine compared to chlorine
low enthalpy of dissociation of \(\mathrm{F-F}\) bond and high hydration enthalpy of \(\mathrm{F^-}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q53 - Stability order of halogen oxides

questiontext.text: What is the general decreasing order of stability of oxides formed by chlorine, bromine, and iodine?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The stability of halogen oxides depends on bond polarisability (favouring iodine) and \(d\)-orbital multiple bonding (favouring chlorine).

Step 2: Middle-Row Anomaly of Bromine
Iodine oxides are most stable due to greater polarisability of the \(\mathrm{I-O}\) bond; chlorine oxides are stabilised by multiple bonding using \(d\)-orbitals. Bromine lacks both advantages, making bromine oxides the least stable.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The decreasing order of stability of halogen oxides is \(\mathrm{I} > \mathrm{Cl} > \mathrm{Br}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q54 - Reactions of F2 and Cl2 with water

questiontext.text: What are the products formed when \(\mathrm{F_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) react separately with water?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Fluorine is a stronger oxidising agent than oxygen and oxidises water to \(\mathrm{O_2}\), whereas chlorine disproportionates in water.

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equations
For fluorine: \(2\mathrm{F_2(g) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 4H^+(aq) + 4F^-(aq) + O_2(g)}\).
For chlorine: \(\mathrm{Cl_2(g) + H_2O(l) \rightarrow HCl(aq) + HOCl(aq)}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{F_2}\) gives \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\), whereas \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) gives \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and \(\mathrm{HOCl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q55 - Non-existent noble gas compound

questiontext.text: Which one of the following noble gas compounds does NOT exist?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Noble gas compounds are primarily known for xenon (and \(\mathrm{KrF_2}\) for krypton), which have lower ionisation enthalpies. No true compounds of \(\mathrm{Ar}\), \(\mathrm{Ne}\), or \(\mathrm{He}\) are known.

Step 2: Evaluation of Species
\(\mathrm{XeOF_4}\), \(\mathrm{XeF_2}\), and \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\) are well-characterised compounds of xenon. Neon has a very high first ionisation enthalpy (\(2080\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)) and does not form \(\mathrm{NeF_2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{NeF_2}\) does not exist.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q56 - Neutral molecule isoelectronic with ClO-

questiontext.text: With which neutral molecule is the hypochlorite ion (\(\mathrm{ClO^-}\)) isoelectronic?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Isoelectronic species have the same total number of electrons.

Step 2: Electron Count
In \(\mathrm{ClO^-}\), the total number of electrons is \(17\ (\text{for }\mathrm{Cl}) + 8\ (\text{for }\mathrm{O}) + 1\ (\text{negative charge}) = 26\) electrons. In \(\mathrm{ClF}\), the total number of electrons is \(17\ (\text{for }\mathrm{Cl}) + 9\ (\text{for }\mathrm{F}) = 26\) electrons.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
\(\mathrm{ClO^-}\) is isoelectronic with the neutral molecule \(\mathrm{ClF}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q57 - Reaction of xenon fluorides with fluoride acceptors and donors

questiontext.text: Xenon fluorides react with fluoride ion acceptors to form cationic species and with fluoride ion donors to form fluoroanions. What are the products of \(\mathrm{XeF_4 + SbF_5}\) and \(\mathrm{XeF_6 + CsF}\), respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{SbF_5}\) is a strong Lewis acid (fluoride ion acceptor), whereas alkali metal fluorides like \(\mathrm{CsF}\) act as fluoride ion donors.

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equations
\(\mathrm{XeF_4 + SbF_5 \rightarrow [XeF_3]^+[SbF_6]^-}\) and \(\mathrm{XeF_6 + CsF \rightarrow Cs^+[XeF_7]^-}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The products are \([\mathrm{XeF_3}]^+[\mathrm{SbF_6}]^-\) and \(\mathrm{Cs}^+[\mathrm{XeF_7}]^-\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q58 - Complete hydrolysis of XeF4

questiontext.text: Complete hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF_4}\) with water yields which set of products?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Unlike \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\), \(\mathrm{XeF_4}\) undergoes disproportionation upon complete hydrolysis in water, yielding elemental xenon (\(\mathrm{Xe}\), \(0\) state) and xenon trioxide (\(\mathrm{XeO_3}\), \(+6\) state) along with \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\(6\mathrm{XeF_4 + 12H_2O \rightarrow 4Xe + 2XeO_3 + 24HF + 3O_2}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Complete hydrolysis of \(\mathrm{XeF_4}\) yields \(\mathrm{Xe}\), \(\mathrm{XeO_3}\), \(\mathrm{HF}\), and \(\mathrm{O_2}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q59 - Reason for large atomic sizes of noble gases

questiontext.text: Why do noble gases have comparatively large atomic sizes in their respective periods?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Atomic radii of elements that form covalent bonds are measured as covalent radii, whereas monoatomic noble gases do not form covalent bonds with themselves.

Step 2: Radius Comparison
For noble gases, atomic size is expressed as van der Waals radius (half the distance between nuclei of non-bonded adjacent atoms), which is significantly larger than the covalent radius of preceding elements in the same period.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Noble gases have comparatively large atomic sizes because they are monoatomic and their radii are measured as van der Waals radii rather than covalent radii.

answer.text: They have the lowest effective nuclear charge in each period.
Their valence electrons enter a higher principal quantum shell.
They are monoatomic, so their reported radii are van der Waals radii rather than covalent radii.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q60 - Maximum coordination number in IF7 among interhalogens

questiontext.text: Why does iodine form a heptafluoride (\(\mathrm{IF_7}\)), whereas no other halogen forms an \(\mathrm{XX'_7}\) interhalogen compound?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In interhalogen compounds \(\mathrm{XX'_n}\), as the ratio of the radius of the larger central halogen \(\mathrm{X}\) to the smaller terminal halogen \(\mathrm{X'}\) increases, the number of atoms per molecule increases.

Step 2: Radius Ratio Comparison
Iodine is the largest stable halogen and fluorine is the smallest halogen, so the radius ratio \(r_{\mathrm{I}}/r_{\mathrm{F}}\) is the maximum possible among halogens, allowing seven fluorine atoms to pack around a central iodine atom in a pentagonal bipyramidal geometry.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The radius ratio between iodine and fluorine is the maximum among halogens, permitting the formation of \(\mathrm{IF_7}\).

answer.text: Iodine has the highest electronegativity among halogens.
Iodine has the smallest atomic radius among halogens.
Only iodine can exhibit a \(-1\) oxidation state.
The radius ratio between \(\mathrm{I}\) and \(\mathrm{F}\) is the maximum among halogens.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_PBLOCKELEMENTS_MCQ_Q61 - Reaction of uranium with ClF3 for uranium enrichment

questiontext.text: Interhalogen compounds such as \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\) are used in the enrichment of \({}^{235}\mathrm{U}\). What are the products of the reaction \(\mathrm{U(s) + 3ClF_3(l) \rightarrow}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
\(\mathrm{ClF_3}\) acts as a powerful fluorinating agent, oxidising uranium metal to volatile uranium hexafluoride (\(\mathrm{UF_6}\)) while being reduced to \(\mathrm{ClF}\).

Step 2: Balanced Chemical Equation
\(\mathrm{U(s) + 3ClF_3(l) \rightarrow UF_6(g) + 3ClF(g)}\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The products formed are \(\mathrm{UF_6(g)}\) and \(3\mathrm{ClF(g)}\).
